"So, shall I fill the admission form? The early-bird discount ends at six today."
"Can I have the full fee structure in writing first, Pooja ma'am? With the refund rules?"
"It's all standard. Everyone signs today."
"Then it should be easy to print," Kashish said, smiling.
"The discount might go, you know."
"If the course is good, I think it'll still be good tomorrow. I'm also seeing the institute near the metro on Saturday."
"They don't have our results."
"Maybe. I'll compare both."
Pooja sighed and printed two pages. Kashish folded them into a file.
That evening, at the kitchen table, Kashish read every line. The refund rule said nothing was returned after seven days.
Kashish called the next morning. "Is the discount still there?"
"Yes, madam, till month end."

qa.q: What did the refund rule say?
qa.a: The refund rule said nothing was returned after seven days.

qa.q: How was Kashish feeling when Pooja said the discount might go?
qa.a: Kashish felt steady rather than panicked; the smile and the reply that a good course would still be good tomorrow show calm confidence.

qa.q: Which of Kashish's steps protected her best?
qa.a: Asking for the fee structure and refund rules in writing, reading every line at home, and comparing with the other institute before paying.

qa.q: How might Pooja see a buyer who asks for printed terms?
qa.a: Pooja may feel her early-bird push has stopped working, and her sigh suggests she wanted a quick signature, yet she still had to print the pages.

grounding: A young woman asks a course counsellor for written terms, reads them overnight and compares options, and finds the offer is still there the next day.

passage:
Last spring I nearly paid a token amount for a one-room flat in Baner within twenty minutes of seeing it.
The broker, Eshaan, kept checking his phone. "Three more parties are coming at four. Give the token now and it's yours."
My stomach dropped at the idea of losing it. The flat had a balcony. My old place had a wall for a view.
But I said I'd sleep on it and asked him to send the rent agreement draft by email. He didn't like that.
That night I read it twice. The deposit clause was different from what he'd said out loud. On Saturday I saw two other flats, one smaller but with clear terms.
On Monday Eshaan called. "Still available, if you're interested."
I went with the smaller one. I miss that balcony sometimes. I don't miss the knot in my stomach.
Kashish

qa.q: When did Eshaan say three more parties were coming?
qa.a: Eshaan said three more parties were coming at four.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when told about the other parties?
qa.a: Kashish felt a sudden fear of losing the flat; "my stomach dropped" shows the pressure hit hard.

qa.q: Which step revealed the problem with the first flat?
qa.a: Asking for the rent agreement draft by email and reading it overnight showed the deposit clause differed from what Eshaan had said aloud.

qa.q: What does Eshaan's Monday call show about the "three more parties"?
qa.a: The flat was still available days later, so the rush was pressure rather than a real queue, and Eshaan still hoped to close the deal.

grounding: A young adult waits a night, asks for the agreement in writing and compares flats instead of paying under a broker's pressure, and the flat is still there days later.
